title: Email campaign
intro: A short work sample. Answer in your own words, the way you would explain it to a manager.
question: Did the email campaign perform better in Week 2? What would you investigate next?

answer_key.verdict: No. Clicks rose in total, but a smaller share of people who opened the email clicked.

values.change: Down 2 percentage points, a 25% relative drop

answer_key.interpretation: Opens grew 50% but clicks grew only 12.5%, so a smaller share of openers clicked in Week 2.
recommendation_examples_valid: Check whether the email content or call to action changed in Week 2.
Check whether the link worked on all devices, especially mobile.
Break Week 2 down by audience segment, for example new vs existing subscribers.
Check whether a new subject line attracted openers who were less interested in the offer.

recommendation_examples_invalid.why: Contradicts the data. More opens in Week 2 came with a lower click rate.
Not proportionate. A drastic step before anyone knows the cause.

recommendation_examples_invalid.text: Check how many sales we made.
recommendation_examples_invalid.why: Not in the data, and the link to the drop is not explained.

answer_key.note: Valid examples are illustrations, not the only correct answers.

metric_calculation.nudge: Both columns went up. Is comparing totals a fair way to judge the two weeks when the number of opens changed?
metric_calculation.hint: For each week, work out what fraction of people who opened the email clicked the link. Then compare the two weeks.

interpretation.nudge: What does your comparison say about how well the email turned opens into clicks?
interpretation.hint: Ask yourself whether clicks grew at the same pace as opens, and what that says about the email.

recommendation.nudge: What could cause the change you found in the numbers, and how would you check it this week?
recommendation.hint: Think of one thing that could cause a smaller share of openers to click, and how you would check it this week.
